ca_whispering_wall_the.blurb: This south-facing wall stands in the Live Oak Picnic Area of Joshua Tree National Park, a little over a mile east of Jumbo Rocks Campground. It has eight climbs of up to roughly 100 feet, nearly all of them traditional leads plus a single top-rope line. Grades begin near 5.6 and reach the low 5.11s, with the largest group at 5.10, so moderate leaders and people after harder top-ropes can both find something. A couple of the leads are bold. Because the wall takes the sun and is shielded from the west, it works well on cold, windy days. Holds are grainy and a few are loose, though they clean up with traffic.

ca_wild_rose_buttress.blurb: Wild Rose Buttress is a white granite crag just before the dam at South Lake, above Bishop in the Eastern Sierra. It sits on a slope across from the road, above a small stand of aspens. There are eight climbs, mostly traditional crack lines with a few newer face routes and a single bolted line. Grades are concentrated at 5.10, with one easy 5.5 and one 5.11 at the upper end.

ca_3_the_tombstone.blurb: The Tombstone is a buttress within Bear Crag in the Mammoth Lakes area, set just around the corner from Fire Wall and hard to miss once you arrive. Its eight bolted sport lines start at 5.10 and climb into the 5.13 range, with the weight of the grades at 5.11 and 5.12, so it rewards climbers who already have the harder numbers dialled. An unfinished project also stands on the wall. Bear Crag is known for steep, well-bolted climbing, and the walk in from the Rainbow Falls trailhead near Red's Meadow takes in the region of 45 minutes.

ca_scott_cosgrove_memorial_buttress.blurb: This buttress is in Box Canyon West, part of the New Jack City sport climbing zone in the High Desert near Barstow. It has eight climbs, nearly all bolted, with one traditional line. The spread is wide: a very easy line, a few moderates in the 5.7 to 5.9 range, two at 5.11 and one standout at the hard end of the grade scale. Reaching it takes a long walk from the canyon parking, either up the canyon or over a ridge on the Twin Towers trail, finishing with a short scramble below the first route.

ca_pangea_wall_or_pangaea_wall.blurb: Pangea Wall is a tall face in Texas Canyon, the conglomerate dome country of Angeles National Forest in northwest Los Angeles County. The wall is about 200 feet high: a steep overhanging base of roughly 30 feet, then lower-angled ground above, all of it cobbles, knobs and inclusions. There are eight routes mixing sport, trad and some aid-assisted lines, with several running two pitches. Grades run from 5.6 up to 5.10, mostly in the 5.7 to 5.9 band. The conglomerate is fragile when damp, so the wall needs dry conditions before anyone pulls on it.

ca_beach_the.blurb: The Beach is a small face on the Central Coast, in the little valley behind the Wagon Caves wall. The climbing is face moves on small huecos in granular sandstone, and sand can wash into the holds over winter. There are eight short routes, six of them top-rope and two with bolts, graded from 5.7 to 5.10, with most in the 5.8 to 5.9 range. Lead options are limited, so bring a top-rope setup and long slings for building anchors.

ca_emergency_room.blurb: Emergency Room is a corridor in the Central Gorge of the Owens River Gorge, near Bishop in the Eastern Sierra, at around 5,450 feet. It holds eight bolted sport routes, starting at 5.10 and running into the 5.12s; half of them are 5.12. The Central Gorge is the busiest section of the canyon, known for closely spaced sport climbs, so expect company nearby. The corridor is entered from the south by scrambling over talus, and the Central lot sits at the top of a steep gully trail down to the canyon floor.
